accounts.name: Revolution Medicines
accounts.trigger: FDA approved Rasonque (daraxonrasib) for previously treated metastatic pancreatic cancer about six and a half months ahead of its PDUFA date. It is the company's first marketed product.
accounts.why: A clinical-stage biotech just became a commercial company. Its first field team was assembled from reps trained elsewhere, and the early approval compressed whatever launch-training timeline they had planned.
buyers: Head of Commercial Training or L&D
pains: No shared training standard yet across a newly hired team
Certification on a narrow second-line indication has to be airtight and on-label
Limited trainer bandwidth while also building global commercial capability
accounts.emailSubject: Rasonque launch readiness, on a shorter clock
accounts.emailBody:
Hi [First name],

Congratulations on Rasonque. Getting approval six and a half months early is remarkable, and it also compresses the window to get a brand-new field team launch-ready.

When a first commercial team comes from many different companies, getting everyone to one on-label standard quickly is usually the hardest part. Quantified builds realistic AI practice from your approved content, and customers see about 40% faster time to readiness.

Would 20 minutes be useful to see how other oncology launch teams certify reps before their next training wave?

Sasha
accounts.opener: Hi [name], it's Sasha from Quantified, I'll be brief. With Rasonque approved early, I'm guessing launch training got compressed. How are you certifying new reps on the second-line message right now?
accounts.nextStep: Identify Head of Commercial Training in Sales Navigator

accounts.name: Merck
accounts.trigger: FDA approved Lipfendra (enlicitide), the first and only once-daily oral PCSK9 inhibitor, reported in Merck's Q2 2026 results. Exact approval day not confirmed; plotted mid-June.
accounts.why: Merck's stated goal is to "democratize PCSK9," moving a class known for specialist injections into a routine pill. That likely means a much wider set of prescribers and many more conversations to get right.
pains: One message has to work for lipid specialists and primary care alike
Objection handling against statins and injectable PCSK9s
Hard to see whether the message is landing across a very large field force
accounts.play: AI Roleplay by HCP persona, Field AI
accounts.emailSubject: Lipfendra and one message across very different prescribers
accounts.emailBody:
Hi [First name],

Moving PCSK9 from injection to a once-daily pill probably means your reps are now calling on a much wider range of HCPs, from lipid specialists to primary care.

Keeping the message consistent and on-label across that range, and knowing whether it is actually landing, is where large launches tend to lose value. Quantified gives reps realistic practice against each HCP persona using your approved content, and our new Field AI shows message pull-through from real visits.

Open to a short conversation on how you're measuring launch execution so far?

Sasha
accounts.opener: Hi [name], Sasha from Quantified. With Lipfendra reaching primary care as well as cardiology, how are you making sure reps handle both conversations the same way?
accounts.caution: Merck also has an FDA decision on ifinatamab deruxtecan (small cell lung cancer) dated Oct 10, 2026: a second reason to reach out this quarter.

accounts.name: AstraZeneca
accounts.trigger: FDA approved Baxfendy, a first-of-its-kind hypertension drug. Executives have said it could reach $5 billion or more in annual sales.
accounts.why: About five months in, the launch is moving from initial training to sustaining performance. A new mechanism in a crowded category means reps must keep explaining something unfamiliar, consistently, for quarters to come.
buyers: Head of Field Effectiveness or Commercial Excellence
First-line sales managers on the launch team
pains: Knowledge and message drift after launch training ends
Managers cannot observe enough calls to coach everyone
Leadership wants proof the launch message is holding up
accounts.emailBody:
Hi [First name],

Baxfendy is about five months into launch, usually the point where launch training fades and the question becomes whether the message is holding up in the field.

With a first-of-its-kind mechanism, reps are explaining something new to HCPs who already have many hypertension options. Quantified helps cardiovascular teams keep reps sharp after launch with continuous, personalized AI practice and coaching built on your approved content. Customers see about 6x more rep practice.

Worth 20 minutes to compare notes on post-launch reinforcement?

Sasha
accounts.opener: Hi [name], Sasha from Quantified. Five months into Baxfendy, what does reinforcement look like for reps now that launch training is behind them?

accounts.name: Eli Lilly
accounts.trigger: In September 2026 the FDA approved imlunestrant with abemaciclib for ESR1-mutated advanced breast cancer (Sep 18) and Onswik (insulin efsitora alfa).
accounts.why: Two launches in very different therapy areas within weeks of each other. The training organization has to produce realistic practice for oncologists and diabetes prescribers at the same time.
buyers: Learning technology or enablement platform owner
pains: Content production is the bottleneck, not trainer skill
Vendor or agency cycles slow down scenario updates
Inconsistent practice quality across two launch teams
accounts.emailSubject: Two September launches, one training team
accounts.emailBody:
Hi [First name],

With imlunestrant and Onswik both approved in September, I imagine your training teams are supporting two very different launches at once.

The bottleneck we usually hear about is building realistic practice scenarios for each audience fast enough. Quantified's authoring tools turn approved content into AI roleplay scenarios in days, without waiting on outside production cycles.

Would a quick call be useful to see how other large pharma teams handle back-to-back launches?

Sasha
accounts.opener: Hi [name], Sasha from Quantified. With two launches in September, where is your team feeling the most pressure, building content or getting reps certified?
accounts.caution: Why Tier 2: a very large enterprise with likely incumbent tools and a long buying cycle. Multi-thread both therapy-area training leads and coordinate with the AE first.

accounts.name: Ultragenyx
accounts.trigger: FDA granted full approval of Fayuvi (UX111), the first treatment for Sanfilippo syndrome type A and the company's second gene therapy approval.
accounts.why: Rare-disease launches run on small, specialized teams with very few chances to get each specialist conversation right. Those conversations are scientifically complex and emotionally sensitive.
buyers: Head of Commercial Training, Rare Disease
pains: Every rep conversation is high stakes and hard to rehearse
Small team, so slow ramp is costly
Spend will need a clear, measurable return
accounts.play: AI Roleplay, Compliance AI, ROI reporting
accounts.emailSubject: Fayuvi launch and making every conversation count
accounts.emailBody:
Hi [First name],

Congratulations on Fayuvi. A first-ever therapy for Sanfilippo type A is a big moment.

In rare disease, a small team gets very few chances with each specialist, so every conversation has to be precise, empathetic, and on-label. Quantified lets reps rehearse those conversations with realistic AI practice built from your approved materials, and gives leaders measurable readiness data.

Would a brief call make sense to see whether this fits your launch plan?

Sasha
accounts.opener: Hi [name], Sasha from Quantified. With a small team launching Fayuvi, how are reps practicing the specialist conversations before they happen?
accounts.caution: Why Tier 2: in early September a failed late-stage Angelman trial sent shares down about 44% in a day, so budgets are likely under scrutiny. Don't mention it in outreach; lead with efficiency and measurable ROI.
